84	S04.1 {hook} Here is what Tessa is weighing. <!-- claims: — -->

90	S05.1 That gap, about $613 a month, is the fallback: in a tight month, it's the least the 30-year asks of her. <!-- claims: fallback_gap_now; hold: 1.0 -->
91	S05.2 The bigger payment fits her budget today, but only just, and a job change or a big repair could squeeze it. <!-- claims: — -->
92	S05.3 Still, she wants the house paid off in 15 years, so the 30-year only works for her if she pays it like a short loan. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->
93	
94	## S06 — The price of paying the 30-year in 15
95	
96	S06.1 At 7.40 percent, finishing that loan in 15 years takes $2,948 a month. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now, r30_now -->
97	S06.2 That's $120 a month more than the 15-year loan, for the same house and the same 15 years. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now, pay30on15_now -->
98	S06.3 Over those 15 years, the extra adds up to $21,622. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.2 -->
99	
100	## S07 — The stack
101	
102	S07.1 In Tessa's world, that price is a stack of bills beside her house: the stack is what keeping the fallback costs. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->
103	S07.2 It exists because the 30-year carries a higher rate on the same balance, this week 0.67 point higher. <!-- claims: spread_now -->
104	
105	## S08 — Why paying in 15 matters at all
106	
107	S08.1 Paid on its own 30-year schedule, her loan would charge $477,622 in interest. <!-- claims: interest_30full_now; hold: 1.0 -->
108	S08.2 Paid in 15 years, it charges $210,691. <!-- claims: interest_30on15_now; hold: 0.8 -->
109	
110	## S09 — The stack, as a difference
111	
112	S09.1 The 15-year loan charges $189,069, and the difference between those last two totals is exactly the stack. <!-- claims: interest_15_now, interest_30on15_now, extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 0.8 -->
113	S09.2 So the 30-year paid in 15 isn't the same loan as the 15-year: it's the 15-year plus a fallback, and the fallback has a price. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now, extra_vs15_total_now -->
114	S09.3 Is Tessa's stack a normal price for that fallback, or is this week unusual? <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->

116	>>> MID-ROLL 1 (in the 1.5 s hold after S09.3; end of act 1, act-2 question open)

118	=== ACT 2 — JOURNEY: the fallback's price in every week since 1991, and Tessa's plan tested ===
119	
120	## S10 — Real loans, real weeks, and the method
121	
122	S10.1 Many walk-throughs of this question use one assumed rate and treat paying early as the obvious win. <!-- claims: — -->
123	S10.2 Here, a real 15-year loan stands next to the 30-year paid in 15, at the real rates of every week since 1991. <!-- claims: first_week, pay30on15_now; hold: 0.8 -->
124	S10.3 We priced the same $320,000 both ways in each of 1,833 weeks, at that week's own survey rates; how it was built is on screen and in the description. <!-- claims: n_weeks, interest_15_now -->
125	S10.4 Tessa's week is the last of them, and in every earlier week we asked her question: what would the fallback have cost then? <!-- claims: last_week -->
126	
127	## S11 — The gap is not fixed
128	
129	S11.1 The answer comes down to one thing: how far the 30-year rate sits above the 15-year. <!-- claims: spread_now -->
130	S11.2 Since 1991, that gap has run from 0.2 point to 1.0 point. <!-- claims: spread_min, spread_max, first_week; hold: 1.2 -->
131	
132	## S12 — Typical gap
133	
134	S12.1 It averaged 0.57 point, and was at least half a point in about 2 in 3 weeks. <!-- claims: spread_mean, share_spread_ge_050 -->
135	S12.2 Tessa's gap this week sits a little above that average. <!-- claims: spread_now, spread_mean -->
136	
137	## S13 — The smallest stack
138	
139	S13.1 Stand a stack beside every week, and the stacks rise and fall with that gap. <!-- claims: — -->
140	S13.2 The smallest was $6,097, in December 2008. <!-- claims: extra_total_min, extra_total_min_week; hold: 1.0 -->
141	
142	## S14 — The tallest stack
143	
144	S14.1 The tallest was $29,502, in January 2023. <!-- claims: extra_total_max, extra_total_max_week; hold: 1.0 -->
145	
146	## S15 — Tessa's place
147	
148	S15.1 The typical week, the median, priced the fallback at $16,631. <!-- claims: extra_total_median -->
149	S15.2 {peak} [serious] Fewer than 1 in 5 weeks since 1991 put a price this high on it. <!-- claims: share_extra_ge_now, first_week, extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->
150	S15.3 That makes Tessa's fallback expensive by history, not a mistake: what a lower payment is worth in a bad month is something this replay can't measure. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->
151	
152	## S16 — By decade: the 1990s
153	
154	S16.1 Line the weeks up by decade, and the pattern is not the one most people expect. <!-- claims: — -->
155	S16.2 In the 1990s, with the 30-year rate typically near 7.73 percent, the typical fallback cost $15,118. <!-- claims: era1991_median_r30, era1991_median_extra_total -->
156	
157	## S17 — The 2000s
158	
159	S17.1 In the 2000s, with rates near 6.18 percent, it cost about the same: $14,210. <!-- claims: era2000_median_r30, era2000_median_extra_total -->
160	
161	## S18 — Lower rates, pricier fallback
162	
163	S18.1 In the 2010s, rates were far lower, typically near 4.03 percent, yet the fallback cost more: $20,374. <!-- claims: era2010_median_r30, era2010_median_extra_total; hold: 1.0 -->
164	
165	## S19 — The gap explains it
166	
167	S19.1 The reason is the gap: in the 2010s and 2020s it typically ran about 0.7 point, against about 0.45 in the 1990s and 2000s. <!-- claims: era2020_median_spread, era2010_median_spread, era2000_median_spread, era1991_median_spread -->
168	S19.2 A lower rate didn't mean a cheaper fallback; a wider gap meant a pricier one. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->
169	
170	## S20 — Since 2020
171	
172	S20.1 Since 2020, the typical week priced it at $21,345, close to Tessa's own stack. <!-- claims: era2020_median_extra_total, extra_vs15_total_now -->
173	S20.2 That's history, not a forecast: the gap has moved before, and nothing here says where it goes. <!-- claims: — -->
174	
175	## S21 — The shortcut (viewer question 2)
176	
177	S21.1 Back to Tessa's own loan, and a shortcut many people reach for: pay the 30-year exactly what the 15-year would cost, and assume it ends on the same day. <!-- claims: pay15_now, pay30on15_now -->
178	S21.2 At this week's rates, it doesn't: it ends after about 195 months, about 15 months late. <!-- claims: months_at_pay15_now, months_late_at_pay15_now; hold: 1.0 -->
179	S21.3 To finish in 15 years, she'd add $733 a month on top of the required payment. <!-- claims: extra_principal_needed_now -->
180	
181	## S22 — The extra doesn't touch the required payment
182	
183	S22.1 That extra never lowers what the loan requires: the required payment stays where it was, and the loan simply ends sooner. <!-- claims: — -->
184	S22.2 That's why the fallback is still there years later, if a month goes wrong. <!-- claims: — -->
185	
186	## S23 — Once a year instead of monthly (viewer question 3)
187	
188	S23.1 Tessa has another practical question: could she send the extra once a year instead of every month? <!-- claims: — -->
189	S23.2 At this week's rates, that's $8,792 once a year, the same total as the monthly extra. <!-- claims: yearly_lump, extra_principal_needed_now -->
190	S23.3 Paid that way, the loan ends four months later. <!-- claims: yearly_lump_months; hold: 0.8 -->
191	
192	## S24 — What the timing costs
193	
194	S24.1 And it charges about $8,200 more in interest, because each dollar sits on the balance longer before it arrives. <!-- claims: yearly_vs_monthly_interest; hold: 1.0 -->
195	S24.2 Monthly or yearly is a cash-flow choice; the replay only prices the timing. <!-- claims: — -->
196	S24.3 Which leaves the question underneath all of this: when Tessa puts an extra dollar into the mortgage, what does it actually earn? <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.5 -->
197	
198	>>> MID-ROLL 2 (in the 1.5 s hold after S24.3; end of act 2, act-3 question open)

201	=== ACT 3 — ANSWER: the bar, Leo, and the threshold ===
202	
203	## S25 — The bar (viewer question 1)
204	
205	S25.1 Every extra dollar of principal stops interest from being charged on that dollar, at the loan's own rate. <!-- claims: bar_now -->

Every cluster has a hold of ≥ 1 s inside it, and each pair is a min/max or a decade pair that is also on screen (B11, B13–B14, B16–B17, B26–B28). Cheapest fix if REVIEWER asks: dates ("December 2008", "January 2023", "November 1994") on screen only.

**Line format.** `Sxx.n {role} [emotion] narration <!-- claims: id, id; hold: s -->`. One sentence per line. Roles on every sentence starting before 1:00. Emotion tags (4): S02.1 `[curious]`, S15.2 `[serious]` (the `{peak}` line), S30.3 `[thoughtful]`, S33.3 `[thoughtful]`. `hold` = silence in the edit. Visuals and on-screen text: `beats.md` (same scene ids). Act boundaries are the `=== … ===` lines (the checker reads these, as in Episode 6).

**Characters (all ILLUSTRATIVE, badge on every frame).** **Tessa** = lead (story §2b), built from dossier situation 2 (high-cost metro, large payment, tight budget, "is a 15-year payoff realistic?"): borrows $320,000 in the week of October 8, 2026; 15-year at 6.73 %, 30-year at 7.40 %. **Leo** = counterweight in act 3 only: a 30-year of the same size in the week of January 7, 2021 at 2.65 % (`leo_*`; the same week as `r30_min_week`), paid like a 15-year: smaller stack ($13,231, about $74 a month), bigger fallback (about $793 a month), bar only 2.65 %.
- Tessa's question (S02.1): *"A 15-year mortgage, or a 30-year paid off in 15 years anyway, with its lower payment kept for a bad month?"* → method: S10.4 "Tessa's week is the last of them, and in every earlier week we asked her question" → final line, hers (S33.3): *"Her answer: the 30-year paid in 15 is the 15-year plus a fallback, and this week, that fallback costs her $120 a month."*
- Peak (S15.2, `{peak}`, 14 words): *"Fewer than 1 in 5 weeks since 1991 put a price this high on it."*

**Core number:** `extra_vs15_total_now` — "$21,622" in digits once (S06.3, fact), then in words as **"the stack"**: S07.1 / S09.1 (what it is: the price of the fallback, the difference between two interest totals), S15.2–S15.3 (comparison: fewer than 1 in 5 weeks as high; expensive by history, not a mistake), S20.1 (close to the 2020s typical), S30.4 (Leo's short stack vs hers), S31.2 (threshold: any borrower's stack comes from the gap between their two offers), S33.1 (callback image). Second recurring object: **"the bar"** (`bar_now`, 7.40 % a year, before taxes), S25–S33.

**Central object (thumbnail G1):** **"the stack"** — a W2 stack of bills (fixed bundle size) beside Tessa's house. Second: **"the bar"** (W3 beam at the loan rate).

**Claim-risk applied (`topics-r2/machine/debt-1/claim-risk.md` + numbers.md speaking rules):** no advice: S03.3 "won't say which loan to take, or whether to invest", S32.7; the price is set *next to* the flexibility, never judged: S05.1–S05.2, S15.3 "expensive by history, not a mistake", S31.3 (a dollar in the house is hard to get back); "history, not a forecast": S03.2, S20.2 ("nothing here says where it goes"), S32.7; "US only": S03.2, S32.7; current numbers only at this week's survey rates on $320,000: S03.1, S32.6; the gap is never "always 0.6": S11.2 (0.2 to 1.0 point), S12.1 (average 0.57, at least half a point in about 2 in 3 weeks); principal and interest only, no taxes, insurance, PMI, deductions: S32.3; prime-borrower survey averages, points and fees differ: S32.2; value of the fallback not measured: S15.3, S32.5; "each extra dollar earns 7.40 %" = interest no longer charged, before taxes, not an investment return, no market comparison: S25.2–S25.3, S32.4; no market return is stated anywhere (none in numbers.md); "we" = analysts only; no imperatives (checker).

**Checker edits (`# TẬP` lines only):** CAST = Tessa, Leo · CORE = `extra_vs15_total_now` / `21,622` · FULL_FORM = PMI → "private mortgage insurance" (only the full form is spoken, S32.3) · WORD_EXEMPT = `\b(1990|2000|2010|2020)s\b` (decade names; the decade medians are `era1991_*` … `era2020_*`, and "1990" is not a numbers.md token). BANNED_NAMES unchanged (Tessa, Leo not in it). Constants unchanged.

**Statements without a numbers.md number (qualitative, for REVIEWER):** S01.2 / S05.2 Tessa's city and budget (ILLUSTRATIVE, dossier situation 2); S10.1 competitor weakness ("one assumed rate … obvious win", dossier: 6/6 top videos use fixed assumptions; no channel named); S13.1 "the stacks rise and fall with that gap" (the weekly price is a function of the two rates; B13 shows it); S16.1 "not the one most people expect" (rhetorical); S22.1 the required payment on a fixed-rate loan does not drop with extra principal (standard amortization, no recast; not modeled beyond the definitions); S24.1 "each dollar sits on the balance longer" (mechanism of `yearly_vs_monthly_interest`); S28.1 "only about 1 week in 5" reads `share_r30_ge_now` = 19 %; S31.3 liquidity (claim-risk: value not measured); S32.2 "strong credit and a large down payment" (claim-risk data limit; the "20 %" is not spoken because no claim carries it).

**Claims wanted:** none required. Optional: the down-payment assumption of the survey as a claim (would let S32.2 say "about 20 percent down").
